experiments.keywords: plant plants light sunlight grow growth bean seed seeds photosynthesis
experiments.title: Do plants need light to grow?
experiments.question: Do bean seedlings grow better in light than in the dark?
experiments.hypothesis: I think the seedling in the light will grow taller because plants use sunlight to make food.
materials: a sunny window and a dark cupboard
steps: Plant 2 bean seeds in each cup, same soil, same depth.
Put one cup on a sunny window and the other in a dark cupboard.
Give both the same amount of water every day.
Measure the height of the seedlings every 2 days for 2 weeks.
Write the heights in your results table.
experiments.measure: height of the seedling in cm
experiments.same: soil, water, seeds, cup size, temperature

experiments.keywords: water evaporation evaporate dry dries sun shade cycle puddle
experiments.title: Where does water evaporate fastest?
experiments.question: Does water evaporate faster in the sun or in the shade?
experiments.hypothesis: I think the water in the sun will dry up first because heat makes water turn into vapour.
materials: a sunny spot and a shady spot
steps: Pour the same amount of water (for example 50 ml) in each saucer.
Mark the water level with the marker.
Place one saucer in the sun and one in the shade.
Check every hour and write how much water is left.
Stop when one saucer is dry.
experiments.measure: amount of water left (ml) after each hour
experiments.same: saucers, amount of water, start time

experiments.keywords: absorb absorbent paper towel cloth sponge material soak soaks
experiments.title: Which material soaks up the most water?
experiments.question: Which material absorbs the most water: cloth, paper towel or sponge?
experiments.hypothesis: I think the sponge will soak up the most because it has many tiny holes.
materials: a piece of cloth, paper towel and sponge of the same size
steps: Pour 100 ml of water in a bowl.
Put in the first material for 10 seconds.
Take it out, squeeze it into the jug and measure the water left in the bowl.
Repeat for each material with fresh water.
Calculate how much each one absorbed.
experiments.same: size of material, time in water, starting water

experiments.keywords: float sink floating sinking density buoyancy objects water
experiments.title: What floats and what sinks?
experiments.question: Do heavy things always sink?
experiments.hypothesis: I think small heavy things will sink and big light things will float.
materials: a stone, coin, cork, leaf, plastic lid, metal spoon, wax candle, orange
steps: Guess for each object: float or sink?
Place each object gently in the water.
Record what happened.
Count how many guesses were right.
Try the orange with and without its peel and explain.

experiments.keywords: magnet magnets magnetic metal iron attract
experiments.title: Which things does a magnet attract?
experiments.question: Which household things are magnetic?
experiments.hypothesis: I think all metal things will stick to the magnet.
materials: a nail, coin, key, aluminium foil, paper clip, spoon, plastic comb, button
steps: Predict for each object: attracted or not?
Touch the magnet to each object.
Record the results in a table.
Find out which metals are magnetic.

experiments.keywords: hand germs wash soap hygiene clean bacteria
experiments.title: Does soap really clean hands?
experiments.question: How well does soap remove dirt compared to water only?
experiments.hypothesis: I think washing with soap will remove more dirt than water only.
materials: cooking oil or a little mud
steps: Put the same small amount of oil or mud on both hands.
Wash one hand with water only for 20 seconds.
Wash the other hand with soap and water for 20 seconds.
Dry each hand on its own paper towel and compare the marks.
Explain what you see.
experiments.measure: how much dirt is left (none, a little, a lot)
experiments.same: time (20 seconds), amount of dirt, amount of water
